If you collect Pokémon or One Piece in Australia, you've probably noticed Japanese booster boxes turning up more and more. Some people swear by them. Others aren't sure what they're actually getting. This is the plain version: how Japanese sealed differs from English, what it really costs to get a box into Australia, which sets I've got right now and how delivery works.

Japanese vs English sealed: what's actually different

The box itself

A Japanese box is not a Japanese-language copy of an English box. The product is built differently.

  • Pokémon. A standard Japanese expansion box is 30 packs of 5 cards. An English booster box is 36 packs of 10. Japanese "high class" sets, such as Terastal Festival ex, come as 10 packs of 10 cards instead.
  • One Piece. Japanese and English boxes both hold 24 packs, but a Japanese pack has 6 cards and an English pack has 12.

Fewer cards per box is the main reason a Japanese box costs less than its English equivalent. It's a smaller product, so compare them per box, not per pack.

Print quality

Japanese cards have a long-standing reputation among collectors for cleaner centring, fewer print lines and a slightly different finish on the holos. In my experience that reputation is mostly earned. But I won't promise any individual card is perfect, because factory variation exists in every language. If centring matters to you, it matters in both languages.

The card stock and backs are different too. Japanese Pokémon cards have a different back from English cards. That's worth knowing if you ever plan to mix them in a binder or a sleeve set.

Pull rates

Here's the honest answer: neither The Pokémon Company nor Bandai publishes pull rates for Japanese product. Anyone quoting you exact odds is guessing or working from a small sample. Collectors widely report that Japanese boxes feel more consistent from box to box. I'm not going to put numbers on it that I can't back up.

Release timing and exclusives

Japanese sets usually release months ahead of the English version. Some sets and special boxes are only ever printed in Japanese. The English sets often combine Japanese releases, so the set names and codes don't line up one to one. That's why every box in the store carries its Japanese set code (M6, sv8a, OP-17 and so on). You can check exactly which release you're buying.

Playing vs collecting

Japanese cards have Japanese text. Most Australian buyers open them for the pulls and the art, or keep the box sealed. If you want cards for local tournaments, check your event's rules on Japanese-language cards before you buy.

What it costs to land a box in Australia

The yen price you see on a Japanese retailer's site is only the start. By the time a box reaches your door in Australia, these costs are in it:

  • The box. The yen price in Japan.
  • The exchange rate. Yen to Australian dollars on the day the order is paid.
  • Freight. A full booster box is a proper parcel, not a letter. International tracked freight from Japan is a real part of the price, especially for a single box.
  • Insurance. A sealed box is worth insuring on the way over.
  • Selling costs. Card processing and platform fees on the sale.

The import freight from Japan is already in every HOKO box price, in Australian dollars. The only thing added at checkout is the local leg: a flat $15.25 Australia Post tracked parcel from Victoria to your door.

GST and the A$1,000 line

Australia treats imported goods differently either side of A$1,000 per consignment.

  • A$1,000 or less. The parcel clears without a customs bill to the buyer at the door. One box sits well under that line.
  • Over A$1,000 in a single consignment. The parcel goes through formal import clearance, and GST, any applicable duty and an import processing charge are assessed before it's released.

So if you're planning a multi-box order, the total can cross that line. Message me before you order and we'll talk through how it ships.

What to buy in 2026

I'm not going to tell you a box is an investment. Nobody knows that, and sealed product goes down as well as up. What I can tell you is how I'd think about it.

  • Opening for the pulls: start with the newest sets. That's where the chase cards people are actually looking for are, and where the singles market is most active.
  • Keeping it sealed: older sets that are already out of print in Japan are the ones that get harder to find. Buy what you'd be happy to own either way.
  • Trying Japanese for the first time: a standard Pokémon expansion or a main One Piece set is the easiest place to start. Save the premium and extra boxes for once you know you like the format.
  • Checking value before you buy: look at recent eBay sold listings for the chase cards from that set, not asking prices. Anyone can list a card for anything.

Japanese or English of the same set?

If a set exists in both languages, ask yourself what you want at the end. If you want to grade the hits or keep a clean binder, Japanese is a good place to start. If you want to play at an English-language event, or you'd rather read the cards, buy English. And if you're chasing one specific card, it's usually cheaper to buy that single than to open boxes hoping for it, in either language. Opening is for the fun of opening.

Japanese Pokemon cards aren't just translated versions of English cards — they have their own sets, exclusive cards, different rarity structures, and a collector market with its own dynamics. Here's what Australian collectors need to know.

What's Different About Japanese Cards?

Different set structure

Japan gets its own set releases that are often smaller and more frequent than the English equivalents. English sets are typically assembled from 2–3 Japanese sets. This means:

  • Japanese sets come out 3–6 months before their English equivalent
  • Some Japanese cards are exclusive and never appear in English releases
  • Pull rates in Japanese sets are often better than English equivalents (you pull chase cards more frequently)

Different card size

Japanese Pokemon cards are slightly smaller than English cards (Japanese: 59×86mm vs English: 63×88mm). They need Japanese-size sleeves. They cannot fit in English toploaders comfortably — use Japanese-size toploaders or team bags.

Language

Card text is in Japanese. Playability-wise this doesn't matter for collectors who don't play competitively, but it does matter if you're trying to enter events. Most casual play groups are fine with Japanese cards.

Rarity symbols

Japanese sets have their own rarity designations. Some rarities that exist in Japanese have no direct English equivalent. Understanding Japanese rarities helps you know what you're buying:

  • ◆ (Diamond) = Common
  • ◆◆ = Uncommon
  • ◆◆◆ = Rare
  • ◆◆◆◆ = Double Rare (equivalent to English ex/VMAX)
  • ★ (Star) = Various ultra-rare tiers
  • ★★ = Two-star — typically the Art Rare / AR equivalent
  • ★★★ = Three-star — the Super Rare / SIR equivalent (often the most beautiful cards)
  • ☆ (Promo Star) = Special Art Rare equivalent

Why Japanese Cards Can Be Better Value

Japanese equivalents of English chase cards are often significantly cheaper:

  • Japanese Umbreon VMAX equivalent: significantly less than the English alt art in many cases
  • Japanese SIR cards are often 30–60% cheaper than English equivalents for the same artwork
  • Japanese booster boxes hold fewer cards than English boxes, so compare them per box, not per pack

The premium on English cards comes from: larger English-speaking market, easier to grade and resell, and English being the "default" for most Australian collectors.

If you're collecting for display and enjoyment rather than resale, Japanese often gives you more card for your money.

Japanese Exclusives Worth Knowing

Pokemon Card 151 (2023)

A Japanese set celebrating the original 151 Pokemon. Contains beautiful alternate art cards for many Gen 1 Pokemon that were never released in English in this form. The Charizard ex SIR and Mew ex SIR from this set are popular worldwide.

VMAX Climax (2021)

Japanese exclusive set containing Character Rare versions of popular Pokemon with trainers — beautiful, unique artwork not available in English. The Character Rare cards (showing Pokemon with their trainer partners) are among the most collected Japanese-exclusive cards.

High Class Packs

Japan releases annual "High Class" sets (formerly called "Gym" sets) that include special art treatments exclusive to Japanese releases. These have no English equivalent and are increasingly collected internationally.

Promos

Japan has an extensive promo card programme — store promos, event promos, campaign promos. Many of these never reach Australian retail and can only be obtained from Japanese sellers. Pikachu promos especially are endlessly collected.

Sourcing Japanese Cards in Australia

  • Online from Japan: Mercari Japan and Yahoo Auctions Japan are where most Japanese collectors sell. You'll need a forwarding service (Buyee, Zenmarket, From Japan) to purchase and ship to Australia. Allow 2–4 weeks and factor in shipping ($20–60 AUD depending on parcel size).
  • Australian sellers: Some Australian TCG stores and eBay sellers stock Japanese cards. Price will be higher than ordering from Japan yourself, but shipping is domestic and faster.
  • At HOKO: We source Japanese product directly and stock Japanese singles and sealed. Check our Pokemon collection with language filter, or email support@hokocollectables.com if you're after specific Japanese cards.

For boxes, the Japanese Sealed collection is the current list: factory-sealed boxes like Mega Symphonia (M1S), imported from Japan by HOKO and dispatched tracked from Victoria.

Grading Japanese Cards

Japanese cards can be graded by PSA and CGC. The grading process is identical to English cards. However:

  • PSA 10 Japanese cards often sell for less than English PSA 10 equivalents (smaller resale market)
  • But Japanese card quality is often higher out of the pack — tighter printing tolerances and less edge whitening make PSA 10s more achievable
  • Japanese-only cards (exclusives) in PSA 10 can be extremely valuable due to scarcity of graded examples

Should You Collect Japanese Cards?

Yes if: You want more card for your money, you love the artwork and don't need English text, you're interested in Japan-exclusive content, or you're sourcing from Japan directly.

Stick to English if: You want maximum resale liquidity in Australia, you play competitively, or you're focused on vintage (English vintage cards have a larger collector market).

Many collectors do both — English for the core collection, Japanese for specific art variants or sets that are better value in Japanese.
